In this module, we are going to add to our knowledge of them, learn a new one, as well as learn how we synthesize and digest them, but first, I want to make sure we remember what we learned in module 1.

Did that jog your memory? I hope so! Let's go over each lipid type again, this time, filling in a bit more detail.

Fatty Acids

In module 1, we discussed triglycerides or triacylglycerides, which is fitting for their structure. They are, after all, three fatty acid chains attached to the acyl group of a glycerol, right? Well, in this module, we are going to discuss triglycerides, but I really want to focus on the fatty acids (FAs), which are the building blocks of the triglycerides. Sometimes the terms are used interchangeably, and while they are similar, they are not the same thing...

Start with Professor Dave and then we will talk about it. You can stop before he talks about terpenes, since we won't be talking about these.
Professor Dave Fatty AcidsOpen on YouTube

Fatty Acids vs. Triglycerides

Let's start here so you can understand why I say they are "kinda" the same thing, and why I am shifting terms on you.

Click on the two hotspots in the photo below to learn the difference between a fatty acid and a triglyceride.

• Fatty Acid

    Fatty acids are chains of carbon atoms with a methyl (-CH3) group at one end and a carboxylix acid (-COOH), hence the acid part of fatty acid, group at the other end.

    The length of the chain can vary. We can also link various structures to the other end via ester bonds. More on these two options later.

    The fatty acid is actually the derived lipid, coming from the hydrolysis of the common version of the lipid itself (the triglyceride)

  • Triglycerides

    The storage form of fatty acids is a triglyceride molecule. This is technically three fatty acid molecules combined together by a glycerol backbone. So, it is not exactly the same as a fatty acid because a fatty acid is just one part of a triglyceride molecule; however, for metabolic purposes, and outside of biochem, people often use the terms interchangeably since the part we care about is the fatty acid and the triglyceride is just how we are storing the fatty acid.

    We store these fatty acids in our adipose tissue.

Health Benefits of Fats

As we already know, fats provide high energy (twice as much energy as carbohydrates) for long term use, but did you know they have lots of other health benefits as well?

  • As we discussed in the last module, adipose tissue, where we store our fat, is our thermal insulation, maintaining the temperature for our subcutaneous tissues and vital organs.
  • Not only are fats thermal insulators, but they are also electrical insulators, making up the myelin shealth around our nerve cells, which allows for rapid passage of action potentials down long axons. This is vital for quick communication between nerves.
  • Many vitamins and nutrients are non-polar, which means they are not going to be able to dissolve in water. In these cases, in order for our body to absorb them, we need them to dissolve in fat. Have you ever had a medication that said to take it with food? This could be the reason why!
  • Fats, especially omegas, also assist with hormone production, blood clotting, brain function, cholesterol transport, and inflammation just to name a few.
    • One type of fat you might have heard of is known as a prostaglandins. They act as a hormone found in almost every mammalian tissue. They trigger the inflammatory reponses in cases of injury and illness, blood flow for blood clotting, and help induce labor.

Naturally Occurring vs. Man-Made Fats

Let's check out the different types of fatty acid arrangement options, starting with the ones you should already know.

Saturated Fatty Acids

Saturated Fatty Acids contain no double bonds, but all carbon-carbon single bonds.

I always remember they are saturated because they have the full amount of hydrogens/bonds possible. They cannot take anymore on. They are saturated with hydrogens.

Saturated FAs have higher melting temperatures. This makes them solid at room temperature.

Saturated FAs are typically your animal fats.

What is an example of a saturated fatty acid?

Cis Fatty Acids

Cis Fatty Acids are naturally occurring unsaturated fatty acids.

An unsaturated fatty acid contains one or more double bonds.

A monunsaturated fat contains a single double bond. As I mentioned in module 1, these fats, also known as MUFAs, are very healthy fats. They can be found in nuts, olives, and avocados and are known for fighting visceral body fat-the bad fat that wraps around your organs. Eat more of these.

A polyunsaturated fat contains two or more double bonds.

When fats are unsaturated in nature, they are almost always in the cis formation.

As we said, saturated fats have higher melting temperatures because they are more tightly packed. This means unsaturated fats have lower melting temperatures because they are loosely packed.

Cis unsaturated fats are liquid at room temperature.

Cis unsaturated fats are typically plant-based fats.

What is an example of a cis unsaturated fat?

Trans Fatty Acids

When fats are saturated during food processing, this is a man-made saturation, not a naturally occurring saturation. In these instances, the double bonding typically occurs in the trans formation rather than the cis formation, hence, the formation of trans-(unsaturated) fats.

The issue with trans fats is their structure actually makes them harder to breakdown. They end up with an even higher melting point than saturated fats, and are likely to end up staying solid, clogging arteries and leading to cardiovascular disease.

So, if we want to avoid transfats, what foods do we need to avoid? Transfats are often found in shortenings and margarines, or any time a traditionally liquid fat is turned into a solid fat. This includes any foods associated with these items, like fried foods and baked goods as well.

Transfats also hide under another name: partially hydrogenated oil... This one you find in peanut butter a lot. This is a process food packaging companies use to increase the shelf life of products, but it converts the cis bonds to trans bonds, so it's just as bad. Stay away.

Omega-3 Fatty Acids

The last one are omega-3 fatty acids, which are a type of unsaturated fatty acid that is super healthy and great for brain and nervous system power. This is where the double bonding starts on the third carbon from the end of the chain.

Can you guess what an Omega-6 FA is then?

Several of these are essential, meaning we must obtain them in our diet because we do not produce them ourselves even though they are essential for our health. Fish and nuts are great sources of omega-3s.

Complex Lipids

Complex lipids are any lipid that have the typical alcohol and one or two fatty acids plus another group on them. They often have a nitrogen containing base as well, but it is that "other" group that makes them complex. In module 1, we introduced you to the main group of complex lipids: phospholipids. What do you recall about them?

Phospholipids

  • The "other" added on is a phosphate group
  • The alcohol for phosphlipids is typically glycerol. In this case, they will have two hydrophobic fatty acids.
    • We refer to them as phospholipids, but they are technically glycerophospholipids.
    • This is the primary component of cell membranes.
    • Other phospholipids are imporant surfactants and one even plays an active roll in apoptosis.
  • We can replace the glycerol with a sphingosine, and that gives us our sphingosphospholipid.
    • These have one fatty acid and one long end of the sphingosine to make the other hydrophobic tail
      • They are also major components of cell membranes, making up lipid rafts for compartmentalization, cell signaling, and transport.
    • A common sphingolipid is sphingomyelin, a component of myelin sheath wrapping around neurons (yes, the same as mentioned with fats above. They work together given that these have fatty acids on them)

Glycolipids

  • If the "other" is a sugar instead of a phosphate, we get a glycolipid.
  • Technically, these are also sphingolipids, can you guess why?
    • The alcohol in them is also a sphingosine. This means they also have one FA.
      • Yep, we can also call them spingoglycolipids.
  • Glycolipids are another important membrane protein. They attach to carbohydrates on the outer parts of the membrane as part of the glycocalyx.
    • Once thought to only be a part of bacterial cells, a glycocalyx is being found in more and more mammalian cells. It is for adhesion to other cells and surfaces as well as a protective barrier, like a glue trap for pathogens trying to enter.
  • A common glycolipid found in animal tissues, galactosylceramide, plays an important role in the myeline of the nervous tissue, just like other lipids we have been discussing.

    FOOD FOR THOUGHT: Galactosylceramide can be broken down to release the sphingosine group and fatty acid, which in this case is cermide. You might have heard of this as the active ingredient in the lotion Cera-V. Given what we just learned about how glycolipids create protective barriers, why do you think this could be helpful for your skin, or at least promoted as helpful for your skin?

NOTE: There are other complex lipids we are not covering. Lipoproteins, sulfolipids, and aminolipids are all named in the book. I just want you to focus on these two groups because I want you to know their importance in cell membranes.

In this case, the videos are optional because the one only covers phospholipids and the other does a good job of listing the various types of complex lipids, but doesn't add much outside of what I am sharing with you. Several people group these with cholesterol because they are all molecules that make up cell membranes, which we will talk about shortly.

Steroids

The last group of lipids are steroids. The video below is great, but don't get bogged down too much on the structure. I don't need you to know the details that you should have learned in organic chemistry. I want you to know the basics (we will cover them following the video), and then the examples outlined at the end of the video.
Professor Dave SteroidsOpen on YouTube

Structure

All steroids have four rings. Three of them have six carbons and one has five carbons. Because of asymmetry in the molecule itself, there are lots of stereoisomers that are possible.

Cholesterol

The most commonly known steroid is cholesterol. The word cholesterol, just like fat, tends to be associated with negative thoughts. But cholesterol is actually important. Just like everything else we have talked about in this lesson, it plays a major role in cell membranes. Cholesterol helps to maintain the fluid state of the membrane by acting as stopgaps for the lipids-as temperature drops, they cannot get too consolidated to completely solidify because they cannot condense past the cholesterols, and as temperatures increase, the membrane does not melt away because the lipids cannot separate more than the distance of the cholesterols. Surprisingly (or not), although cholesterol is widely distributed in all cells, it is found most in nervous tissue.

Other Important Steroids

Sex hormones are steroids too! Estrogens, androgens, and progresterones are all important steroids. These are going to facilitate puberty and standard development in men and women, as well as menstrual cycles and pregnancy.

Cortisol is important for inflammation, metabolism, and stress response.

Bile acids are necessary for steroids synthesized in the liver and are digestive surfactants. They help to digest, well lipids.

Introduction

We know that fats are high in energy. We already discussed how they are a more efficient form of energy than carbohydrates, right? But, what did we learn in the last lesson? Fatty acids are stored as triglycerides and those triglycerides are stored in our adipose tissue. So what happens when you are exercising, and you need energy in your muscles? How does it get from a triglyceride in your adipose tissue to ATP in your muscle? That's what we are going to talk about in this lesson. Fatty acid degradation is a three step process:

1. Release of free fatty acids from the triglycerides so we can send them out into our blood stream.

2. Activation of the fatty acids so they can enter the mitochondria

3. Breakdown of the fatty acids. This is going to be the bulk of our lesson. Do you remember what we are going to make? All roads lead to the same place...

Let's dive in.

Steps 1 and 2. Release, Transport, and Activation of Free Fatty Acids
Steps 1 and 2 of FA degradationOpen on YouTube
Step 1: Lipolysis

The process for breaking down triglycerides into the separate components - glycerol and free fatty acids - is known as lipolysis. It is catalyzed by lipases, which are triggered by a variety of hormonal signals that let the enzymes know energy is needed somewhere. Both the glycerol and fatty acids will be released into the blood stream.

Fatty acids are not water soluble. While in the blood stream traveling to their target tissue, they will be bound to albumin. Once in the target tissue, they will be bound to a fatty acid binding protein.

NOTE: The glycerol from the triglyceride will be taken up by the liver and phosphorylated. It will be converted into either pyruvate or glucose via the glycolytic or gluconeogenic pathway.

Step 2: Activation

Fatty acids are going to be converted into an active intermediate by binding with coenzyme A to form acyl CoA (not to be confused with Acetyl CoA, which we will form in the next step). This is going to require energy from ATP and the help of the enzyme CoA synthetase.

This reaction takes place on the outer membrane of the mitochondria. It shuttles the fatty acid into the intermembrane space of the mitochondria through voltage dependent ion channels. We need one more step to pass through the inner mitochondrial membrane:

The fatty acids combine to the alchol carnitine to form Acyl Carnitine, releasing the CoA, with the help of the enzyme carnitine acyltransferase I.

IMPORTANT NOTE: This is the key regulatory step for FA degradation. Various hormones and products of other metabolic pathways will inhibit carnitine acyl transferase I, blocking the flow of FAs into the mitochondria, therefore halting FA degradation.

Acyl carnitine is then able to be shuttled across the inner mitochondrial membrane by a translocase. Once inside the mitochondrial matrix, a second acyl transferase enyzme (acyl transferase II) reverses the previous reaction, replacing the carnitine with the CoA, and the translocase returns the carnitine to the cytoplasmic side again.

FOOD FOR THOUGHT: What do you think would happen if the fatty acids couldn't enter the mitochondria? There are diseases that result in just that. They are often called carnitine deficiencies. It is believed that an inability to synthesize carnitine contributes to austism in males. This can result in muscle cramping, weakness, and even death. Carnitine is now a popular item in dietary supplements, although there is little evidence that supplemental carnitine does any good.

How'd you do on steps 1 and 2? Feeling pretty good? Let's move onto the final step of fatty acid degradation. This is where all the action is...

Step 3: Beta Oxidation
Step 3 of FA degradation-oxidationOpen on YouTube

Let's break that down. The name of the game is beta oxidation. So, we are going to undergo oxidation reactions. You will see this anytime it mentions the enzyme dehydrogenase or the process of dehydrogenation in the video. It's beta because, as they said, it is happening on the beta carbon. This is going to be a series of four reactions. The number of times we go through these four reactions depends on how long the fatty acid chain is.

Each time we complete the series of reactions, we cut 2 carbons from our fatty acid in the form of Acetyl-CoA. The video you watched talked about a 16 carbon chain, which required 7 rounds of oxidation. The draw with me video linked below is more generic and doesn't use a specific example.

Let's take a look at our four steps:

1. Oxidation

The first step is oxidation via the enzyme acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.

This removes two hydrogen atoms from the fatty acid and simultaneously reduces FAD+ to FADH2.

A new double bond is formed on the fatty acid in place of the hydrogen atoms.

2. Hydration

In step two, water is added to saturate the double bond. This is catalysed by the enzyme enol-coA hydratase.

This added a hydroxyl group to our fatty acid.

3. Oxidation

Step three is oxidation again. This time we are going to dehydrogenate our new hydroxyl group via the enzyme hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase.

This is going to reduce NAD+ to NADH.

We made a new carbonyl group on our fatty acid.

4. Thiolysis

All the stuff we added onto our fatty acid comes together to look a lot like an acetyl-CoA molecule. So, now we cut it off to release an acetyl-CoA.

Then we add a new acyl-CoA to the end of our fatty acid so it is ready for another round of beta oxidation.

This whole thing is catalyzed by the enzyme thiloase.

Summary

In summary, one round of beta oxidation has given us:

-One FADH

-One NADH

-One Acetyl CoA that can go into the citric acid cycle

And that's just for one small part of the fatty acid! The example in both videos was the fatty acid palmitate, which is a 16 carbon fatty acid. That's 7 rounds of oxidation, which is 7 FADH, 7 NADH, and 8 Acetyl CoA (remember, the last split will be a four carbon molecule into two acetyl Co-A molecules with one round of oxidation). After using a whopping two ATP to activate the palmitate, we have 108 ATP we are able to generate, for a net of 106 ATP! Now you can see in action why fats are so much more efficient at providing energy than carbohydrates, and why a little goes a long way!

Modifications for Non-Traditional Fatty Acids

Not all fatty acids are created equal. Before we move on from fatty acid oxidation, we need to talk about the variations that are made for unsaturated fatty acids and very-long-chain or odd-chain fatty acids.

  • In peroxisomes, we sometimes see fatty acids with chains of more than 20 or 22 carbons in length. In these cases, the breakdown of these fatty acids are not for energy purposes, as we would see in the mitochondria, and the end product is not acetyl-CoA, but rather octanoyl-CoA. These peroxisomal fatty acid oxidations are linked to high fat diets and hypolipidemic drugs. Additionally, peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation is found as a pathway to shorten the side chain of cholesterol in bile acid formation.
  • Additional steps are required to oxidize unsaturated fatty acids. Isomerases and reductases are strategically used by our bodies at varying steps in the beta oxidation pathway to rearrange unsaturated fatty acids into isomers that are known intermediates for the pathway.
  • Finally, odd-chain fatty acids are oxidized in much the same way as even-chain fatty acids, except that propionyl CoA, a three carbon molecule, is formed at the end of the final round. Propionyl CoA is then converted into succinyl CoA where it can enter into the citric acid cycle.

Ketogenesis

The last thing we need to talk about in this lesson is the formation of ketone bodies. Do these sound familiar to you? Maybe not directly, but I am sure you have heard of the Keto diet, which is a diet high in fat. Are you starting to make the connection yet?

In a nutshell, most of the fatty acids that are converted into Acetyl CoA then enter into the citric acid cycle; however, when there is an abundance of fatty acid oxidation, the liver will produce ketone bodies, an alternative fuel source, in a process called ketogenesis.

Click on the hotspots in the image below to learn more.

• Ketogenesis

    Ketone bodies are produced in the mitochondria of the liver. The three major ketone bodies are acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutarate, and acetone.

    This happens as a result of a build up of acetyl-CoA during beta oxidation. Acetyl-CoA enters the citric acid cycle, but we are saturating the oxaloacetate/not producing more oxaloacetate to bind with more acetyl-coA, so it builds up. The Acetyl CoA goes on to make ketone bodies instead of waiting in line.

  • Ketone bodies travel

    The acetone is released in the lungs and bladder because it cannot be used to produce energy. This is the "science" behind the keto diets. Fats are being broken down into ketone bodies that are then being released in your breath and urine. This also accounts for "keto breath".

    The others are sent to various tissues that need energy.

  • Ketone bodies become enegy

    The ketone bodies then enter the citric acid cycle in extra hepatic tissues as needed.
Ketogenesis in 2 minutesOpen on YouTube

Dangers of Ketogenesis

While the keto diet sounds great, and it can be, there are risks involved with being in a state of ketosis for too long.

Higher than normal quantities of ketone bodies present in the blood or urine constitute ketonemia or ketonuria, respectively. The overall issues is called ketosis. Ketosis is most common during times of starvation, when there is a long term depletion of available carbohydrates, but it is also seen in long term keto diets. This can lead to something called ketoacidosis, which can dangerously decrease the pH of the blood.

Ketosis is also common in individuals with diabetes mellitus due to their deficient glucose metabolism. This is one of the reasons diabetics must regulate their blood and eating so much because if they do not eat frequently, a drop in their blood pH can happen quickly from ketogenesis.

Acetyl Co-A

Acetyl-CoA of course! All roads lead to Acetyl-CoA. What we are going to see is that fatty acid biosynthesis, AKA lipogenesis (if we are generating NEW fatty acids from non-lipid materials) is essentially just fatty acid degradation in reverse. So where do you think we are going to start?

If you guessed Acetyl-CoA, you are getting good at this game... Acetyl-CoA is the precursor for virtually all fatty acids. We are going to convert it back into palmitate, that 16-carbon fatty acid the videos used as the example in the previous lesson, which will then go on to form a variety of other fatty acids.

Knowing this is going to be degradation backwards, let's see how much you can predict as we go along...

Stage 1: Preparation for Fatty Acid Synthesis

So, this first part we are not calling an actual step in fatty acid synthesis, but instead a pre-step. Let's play a little drag the words to fill in the blanks to see if you can guess what we need to do here.

-Fatty acid degradation takes place in the mitochondria.

-The first step in FA degradation was activation that moved the FA from the cytosol to the mitochondria.

-Knowing FA synthesis is the reverse of degradation, where do you think it is likely to take place? The cytosol.

-We also know the starting material for FA synthesis (and the end product of degradation is Acetyl-CoA), which is located in the mitochondria.

-So the first step of FA synthesis is going to have to be to move it back out of the mitochondria and into the cytosol!

Did you get all that? Fatty acid synthesis takes place in the cytosol. But our starting material, Acetyl-CoA, is in the mitochondria. So, the pre-step is to get the Acetyl-CoA out of the mitochondria and into the cytosol. Easier said than done. This is going to happen through the first step of the citric acid cycle in a process calling the citrate-malate shuttle.

Time to watch a video on how it works and then talk about it.
FA synthesis prepOpen on YouTube

Think back to the regulation of the citric acid cycle discussed in module 3. Remember specifically we said "the enzyme citrate synthase is regulated through feed back inhibition. The product, Citrate, of the first reaction Acetyl CoA + Oxaloacetate --> Citrate will inhibit the reaction itself, therefore stopping the cycle." It does this by moving citrate into the cytosol instead of proceeding to the next step in the citric acid cycle.

The cytosol-living citrate will then be cleaved by the enzyme ATP-citrate lyase, at the expense of an ATP, reversing the initial reaction that generated the citrate in the first place. This results in oxaloacetate and Acetyl-CoA in the cytosol.

NOTE: In order for the oxaloacetate to get back into the mitochondria, it has to be converted to malate because oxaloacetate cannot penetrate the mitochondrial membrane anymore than Acetyl-CoA could. Once back inside the mitochondrial matrix, malate will convert back into oxaloacetate, recreating the final step of the citric acid cycle.

*Notice-this process generates an NADPH. We will be able to use the energy from this molecule to help synthesize the fatty acid. More on this later.*

This preparation phase is stimulated by insulin, which is typically released in times of high blood glucose.

Phase 2 (Step One): Activation of Acetyl-CoA

At this point, we have our starting material, Acetyl-CoA, in the starting position (Cytosol), so we are ready for the first official step of fatty acid synthesis: carboxylation of Acetyl-CoA by the biotin-dependent enzyme acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1. This turns it into its activated form, Malonyl-CoA.

In the video, the activation process runs from about 2:00-3:15. You can zone out from 3:15-4:40 (more detail than you need to know), and then watch from 4:40 to the end.
Acetyl-CoA activationOpen on YouTube
The overall conversion of Acetyl-CoA to Malonyl-CoA requires carbon dioxide in the form of bicarbonate (HCO3-) and the use of energy from ATP.

This reaction is actually a two step process.

1. Carboxylation of biotin.

In this step, the biotin, attached inside of the enzyme will "hold" the carboxyl group from the bicarbonate. This acts as the transfer intermediate for the carboxyl group.

2. Malonyl-CoA formation.

The carboxyl group is then transferred to acetyl-CoA, forming malonyl-CoA.

NOTE: Malonyl-CoA is a 3 carbon molecule. In the next step, we are going to use this molecule to elongate an Acetyl-CoA molecule by adding two of the three carbons onto Acetyl-CoA. We will do this over and over again until we have a 16 carbon fatty acid.

This phase, the activation of Acetyl-CoA, is the primary regulatory step in the lipogenesis pathway. Yes, the previous phase can be regulated through insulin/citrate availability, but this step is irreversible, and therefore commits the Acetyl-CoA to fatty acid biosynthesis.

Let's take a look at a few ways we regulate this step before we move on to what comes next.

Regulation of Fatty Acid Biosynthesis

Fatty acid synthesis is controlled in a few manners that really all lead back to a single manner of regulation: diet.

First, since activation is the key to FA synthesis, regulation has to happen through control of Acetyl-CoA Carboxylase 1. If we cannot generate Malonyl-CoA, we cannot make fatty acids.

FUN FACT: Remember when we talked about FA degradation, I talked about regulation through blocking the transfer of the FA into the mitochondria? Well, what I didn't mention was the most common way the transferase enzyme was inhibited was by the product of a reaction catalyzed by Acetyl-CoA Carboxylase 2!

So, what regulates Acetyl-CoA carboxylase? The absence of citrate or Acetyl CoA in the cytosol would do it, since then we couldn't convert Acetyl-CoA to Malonyl CoA. But more importantly, a variety of hormones are known for lipogenesis regulation, including glucagon, epinephrine, and especially insulin. The change is what is known as an adaptive control, meaning it happens at the gene transcription level.

The main regulatory factory for the rate of lipogenesis is the nutritional state of the organism. In a fed-state, with a diet high in carbohydrates, fatty acid synthesis will be high. In fasted-states, either by restricted caloric intake, high-fat diets, or a deficiency of insult, such as in diabete mellitus, fatty acid biosynthesis will be depressed.

A FEW FUN FACTS:

1. The alterations to Acetyl-CoA Carboxylase happen via adaptive control, meaning at the gene transciption level. Insulin (and moving backwards really high carb diets) trigger the body to not just turn on the current carboxylase enzymes, but to make more carboxylase enzymes, significantly increasing the rate of lipogenesis. These alterations can happen within a matter of days of a diet change.

2. Ethanol will increase the rate of fatty acid synthesis. Ethanol breakdown in the liver results in a release of NADH. That NADH inhibits gluconeogenesis and causes the accumulation of lactate. This can lead to hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis. The NADH will also inhibit fatty acid oxidation and trigger fatty acid synthesis. This causes fatty liver disease (and overall decreases your catabolism and increases fat production).

Think about it

How does activation in FA degradation compare to activation in FA synthesis?

Phase Three: Elongation of the Fatty Acid

Elongation is going to be the part where we add to our fatty acid. Once again, we are going to start with a two carbon Acetyl-CoA, and we are going to add two carbons at a time (from Malonyl-CoA) onto it until we get to a 16-carbon palmitate.

And once again, this is going to look a lot like the opposite of beta oxidation, so let's see if you can figure out what's going to happen.

Think about it

What were the four steps in the oxidation of fatty acids? Do you know the opposite reaction for each one?

That's right folks! This is going to be a series of four reactions:

Condensation--> Reduction--> Dehydration--> Reduction

These are the exact reverse of those we saw in beta oxidation. Each cycle will add two carbons (instead of removing two like we saw in oxidation) to the carbonxyl end of the molecule. This happens at the expense of two NADPH. Let's see it in action.
FA elongationOpen on YouTube

Fatty Acid Synthase

Although we have a series of steps, they are all lumped together as one being controlled by a multifunctional enzyme complex known as Fatty Acid Synthase.

The individual enzymes within the complex are covalently joined together. Why do you think they would do this? Well, it allows for compartmentalization of the process within the cell without the need for permeability barriers, and the synthesis of all the enzymes in the complex is easily coordinated since it is encoded by a single gene. Makes life for this complex easy peazy.

The enzyme complex resides on the cytoplasmic side of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. So, while FA synthesis is still taking place in the cytoplasm, it is technically on the SER as well.

Summary of Completing a Palmitate Molecule

As we mentioned, each round of our final phase will add carbons to our starting Acetyl-CoA. Next question then...

Fill in the blanks

Fill in the missing number (digit, not spelled out)

We need ______ rounds of phase 3 to make our 16-carbon palmitate molecule.

Show answer

We need 7 rounds of phase 3 to make our 16-carbon palmitate molecule.

The synthesis of palmitate requires:

  • 8 molecules of Acetyl-CoA
    • 1 starting Acetyl-CoA and 7 converted to Malonyl-CoA
  • 7 rounds of phase 3 elongation
    • Again, we started with a 2 carbon Acetyl-CoA, so we needed to add 14 more carbons.
  • 7 molecules of ATP
    • One each time we activate Acetyl-CoA to Malonyl-CoA
    • This does not include the ATP required to move Acetyl-CoA out of the mitochondria. Remember, that's a pre-step, not a real step.
  • 14 molecules of NADPH
    • Two per round of elongation
    • Remember, we can generate some of this when we return malate to the mitochondria. The rest comes from the pentose-phosphate pathway.
If you'd like to see the details of how carbons are transferred to elongate, watch this (optional)

The Final Step: Modification

As we mentioned before, fatty acid synthesis is always going to result in a free palmitate. But what if we need a different fatty acid? One that has more or less carbons? One that is unsaturated?

In general, these are all modifications that can happen later on as needed. Further elongation can be stimulated, as can partial degradation of the fatty acid chain. Additional enzymes, such as prostaglandins can introduce double bonds to make unsaturated fatty acids.

FUN FACT: Mammals lack the enzymes to introduce double bonds at carbon atoms beyond C-9 of the fatty acid chain. However, mammals require several such fatty acids, including linoleate and linolenate, which is why they are among the list of essential fatty acids.

Introduction

You may wonder why I am lumping our storage lipids (triglycerides) with our membrane lipids (phospholipids and sphingolipids) into the same lesson. Well, isn't it obvious? What do they have in common? They are fatty acid(s) combined to an alcohol. This means the processes to create them are really going to be almost the same.

In fact, triglycrides and phospholipids start out the exact same because they both involve the addition of the alcohol glycerol. Ok, we need to add fatty acids and glycerol together. In this case, we are going to form Phosphatidate. But before that, let's check out an intro video on the similarities of triglycerides and phosphoglycerides, and when the body would make one over the other.
Triglyceride and Phosphoglyceride VideoOpen on YouTube

Phosphatidate Formation

First things first, we need to find fatty acids and glycerol to combine. We know where fatty acids come from, right? In case you forgot, we had an entire lesson on fatty acid synthesis. We also had a lesson on fatty acid degradation that started with the release of free fatty acids from triglycerides. What else do we get when we release fatty acids from a triglyceride? That's right, a glycerol. So we have the parts we need.

In a nutshell, phosphatidates are diglycercide molecules, meaning we are going to add two fatty acids to a glycerol molecule.

This video will show you how we are going to create our Phosphatidate. For now, you can stop at 3:15, although the final step will be covered in the next section of this lesson.
Phosphatidate formationOpen on YouTube

Step 1: Activation

If you have been paying attention to our previous pathways, you could probably guess what we need to do to get this pathway rolling: Activate. Both the fatty acid and the glycerol need to be activated in order to be ready to react.

Remind me... What is the active form of a fatty acid and what is the enzyme that catalyzes this activation?

  • Acyl-CoA via Acyl-CoA Synthetase
  • Acetyl-CoA via Acetyl-CoA Synthetase
  • Acyl-CoA via Fatty Acid Dehydrogenase
  • Glyceraldehyde via Glyceralydehyde Reductase

Acyl-CoA via Acyl-CoA Synthetase

That's right, for a FA, the active form is Acyl-CoA, as we discussed in FA oxidation, and this is done with the help of the enzyme Acyl-CoA Synthetase.

For glycerol, we need it to be activated into Glycerol-3-Phosphate (G3P) via the enyzme Glycerol Kinase, an enzyme present in the liver, kidneys, intestine, brown adipose tissue, and lactating mammory glands.

FUN FACT: There is another way to get G3P. That is through conversion of dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP or DHA) into G3P. This is what happens in tissues without glycerol kinase, like the muscles. DHAP is touted as a health supplement for improved athletic performance.

Step 2: Acyl Transer (times two)

G3P is then processed into Phosphatidate via two steps catalyzed by acyl transferase.

The other name for Phosphatidate is Diacylglycerol-3-Phosphate because it is a 2 acyl glycerol molecule. Remember, a triglyceride is also known as a triacylglyceride molecule.

From this step, the paths for a triglyceride or a phospholipid diverge.

Biosynthesis of triglycerides and biosynthesis of phospholipids are both going to take place on the cytosol side of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum

SIDENOTE: What else takes place here?

Although we are going to see different pathways for triglycerides vs. phospholipids, we are going to see similarities for them, as they are following the same general process: both are combining fatty acids with an alcohol and any other modifying units that are needed.

Actually, there are going to be several roads that will lead to varous phospholipids, and triglycerides are going to fall along the pathways in the middle a bit.

Let's dive in.

Biosynthesis of Triacylglycerides

This one will be short. You can see the overview of how we go from Phosphatidate to triglyceride in the remainder of the video above (from 3:15 on).

The completion happens via the triacylglycerol synthetase complex. The two step process involves removing the phosphate from phosphatidate (diacylglcerol-3-phosphate) and adding another fatty acid (this would be a third acyl transferase step).

Triglyceride formation happens primarily in the liver, and then the triglycerides are transported to muscles for fuel or adipose tissue for storage. 85% of our energy is stored as TAGs in adipose tissue.

Biosynthesis of Phospholipids

Phospholipids can get a little hairier because there are a variey of different ones. I want you to understand the overall general process, not the different variations needed for each type of phospholipid.

Check out the two hotspot in the photo below to learn about the activation step in phospholipid formation.

• Phosphatidate Activation

    Either phosphatidate or the alcohol must be activated during phospholipid formation.

    Phosphatidate can be directly activated, as is the case in the formation of cardiolipin and phosphatidylinositol.

    Cardiolipin is produced solely in the mitochondria for mitochondrial membranes. It helps to organize the enzymes in the ETC.

  • Alcohol Activation

    Either phosphatidate or the alcohol must be activated during phospholipid formation.

    Phosphatidate can be combined with an activated alcohol instead of being activated itself, such as when forming phosphatidylcholine or phisphatidylethanolamine. In this case, phosphatidate is first converted to diacylglycerol (by removing a phosphate) just as if we were forming a triglyceride!

Recall that phospholipids (AKA phosphoglycolipids) vary based on the alcohol attached to the phosphate group. The formation of each type will require various enzymes and reactions based on what groups are needing to be added.

Let's use the formation of phosphatidylcholine as our example since this is the most common phospholipid, comprising up to 55% of our membranes.

In order to create phosphatidylcholine, we need the enzyme choline kinase and two transferase steps, as shown in the image above. That pathway is happening on the left. You can also see in parallel on the right the conversion of phosphatidate to diacylglycerol before it combines with the phosphcholine. You can see there is only a one step difference between the formation of phosphatidylcholine vs. triacylglycerol.

What else do you notice in looking at this reaction? It requires ATP! This is an anabolic reaction, remember, so we need energy input to build molecule. Can't forget the basics.

FUN FACT: Phosphatidylcholine is such an important phospholipid that there is actually a second way that our bodies have developed to generate it. We can convert phosphatidylethanolamine directly into phosphatidylcholine when needed!

Regulation

In general, formation of triglycerides and phospholipids is controlled by the availability of free fatty acids. Without free fatty acids, no lipids can be generated.

However, the control of which lipids will be generated lies at the split between phosphatidate and diacylglycerol, which is controlled by the enzyme phosphatidic acid phosphatase (PAP). When active, PAP generates diacylglycerol, which can react with activated alcohols to form phospholipids or with fatty acyl CoA to form triacylglycerols. When PAP is inactive, phosphatidate is used for the synthesis of different phospholipids. PAP also controls the amount of DAG and phosphatidate, both of which function as second messengers.

Biosynthesis of Sphingolipids

The final type of lipid that is included in this lesson is a sphingolipid. Remember, a sphingolipid starts with a sphingosine instead of a glycerol, which is why they were not created the same way as our triglycerides or phospholipids.

Sphingolipids are found in all membranes, but they are most abundant in nervous tissues. Sohingolipids are formed from ceramide, which is made from palmitoyl-CoA (an activated fatty acid) and serine.

Just as phospholipids can vary, we modify the ceramide as needed to form a variery of sphingolipids. For example, we can combine with phosphorylcholine to create sphingomyelin or we can add sugar to them to form glycosohingolipids. Regardless of the modifications, sphingolipids are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum from the amino acid serine.

Storage and Membrane Lipids in Disease

There are several lipids you may have heard of:

• Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids that are known to be the target binding cite for cholera toxin and enterotoxigenic E. coli (the caustive agent for Traveller's diarrhea).
  • Gangliosides are also an issue in Tay Sach's diease, where we cannot degrade them. This reasults in swollen, lipid-filled lysosomes.
  • Phophatidylcholine binds to form dipalmitoul-phosphatidylcholine in your lung alveoli. This combo is important because it helps reduce surface tension and makes it easier to breathe. Infant respiratory distress syndrome is known to lack these surfactants, leading to struggles with breathing.
  • Multiple Sclerosis is a demyelinating disease with loss of phospholipids and sphingolipids.

Introduction

Welcome to the final lesson of this module. Once again, we are going to have a short lesson.

Cholesterol gets a bad rap, but as we know, it is vital for the stability of our membranes, as well as for the formation of Vitamin D, steroids, and the assistance of fat digestion via bile salts. We can either obtain cholesterol from the diet or synthesize it (the focus of this lesson). The primary site of synthesis is the liver, where it will be used to create bile salts for fat digestion, although it can also be made in the intestines.

What we are going to find is that cholesterol is made from 27 carbons, all of which are derived from the ever important Acetyl-CoA (once again proving that all roads lead to Acetyl-CoA). The pathway is long, so I just want you to know the major steps in the process.

Check out the video first. It covers almost everything you need for cholesterol!
Cholesterol synthesisOpen on YouTube

Steps to Cholesterol Synthesis:

Step 1: Biosynthesis of Mevalonate

In this three step process, two Acetyl-CoA combine to form Acetoacetyl-CoA, which then combines with another Acetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA (3-Hydroxy-3-Methyl-Glutaryl-CoA). HMG-CoA is then reduced to form Mevalonate via the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase.

This last part of first step in which HMG-CoA is reduced to Mevalonate is the commitment step for cholesterol synthesis. It is irreversible and, just as we have seen before, commits Acetyl-CoA to forming cholesterol. It is also the rate-limiting step, which means we are going to use this point to control the rate of cholesterol synthesis.

FUN FACT: Cholesterol is vital to our survival. This is proven by the fact that mice without HMG-CoA reductase, and therefore without the ability to synthesize cholesterol, will die.

Step 2: Formation of Isoprenoid Units
In three sequential phosphorylation steps, mevalonate is converted to isopentenyl diphospate.

Isopentenyl diphosphate is also known as isopentenyl pyrophosphate. It contains five carbons and two phosphate groups.

The formation of this molecule comes at the cost of three ATP (one per phosphorylation step) and requires three kinases. The final step, following the three phosphorylations is a decarboxylation step in which we release carbon dioxide and a phosphate group.

Check yourself

Based on everything we have learned so far, if I told you these first two steps (essentially Acetyl-CoA to Isopentenyl Diphospate) happened in the same place, where would you guess that place would be?

  • the mitochondrial matrix
  • the endoplasmic reticulum
  • the cytosol
  • the inner mitochondrial membrane
Show answer

the cytosol

Step 3: Formation of Squalene

Next we move from the cytoplasm to the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum. Here, six molecules of isopentenyl diphosphate come together through a series of condensation reactions to form squalene.

Squalene is a 30 carbon molecule. The sequence follows the pathway:

C5 ----> C10 ----> C15 ----> C30

One isopentenyl diphosphate will isomerize into dimethylallyl pyrophosphate to allow for the binding of the two isomers, which begins the condensation reaction.

The final step in the squalene formation pathway is a reduction by NADPH.

Cyclization

Step 4: Formation of Lanosterol

Still in the lumen of the ER, squalene is going to begin to fold. It will form a structure close to a steroid nucleus, lanosterol, via a mixed function oxidase, squalene epoxidase.

This process requires oxygen and NADPH.

Step 5: Cholesterol Formation

Finally, on the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum, the final steps of cholesterol formation occur. Bonds and elements within the lanosterol are moved around to be able to remove three carbons and close the rings of the molecule to form a final cholesterol molecule.

Regulation

The rate of cholesterol synthesis is responsive to cellular level feedback through control of the HMG-CoA reductase enzyme.

As we saw in the video, the most common control mechanism is at the molecular level via a sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP) that controls the transcription of the enzyme.

SREBP is inhibited by insulin, meaning HMG-CoA reductase activity, and therefore cholesterol production, increases in the presence of insulin. The same occurs in the presence of thyroid hormone, whereas glycagon and glucocorticoids increase SREBP/decrease HMG-CoA reducatase.

Cholesterol Transport

Cholesterol is made in the liver, but used throughout the body. Remember, cholesterol is a lipid, which means it is going to be insoluble in water. In order for us to carry cholesterol through the blood to the tissues in need, we need carrier molecules, called lipoproteins. There are a variety of different lipoproteins, classified based on their density, and known commonly as either LDL or HDL, which you may have heard of in a health aspect.

Check out this video and then we will talk about them more.
Cholesterol transportOpen on YouTube

Lipoproteins are packages of lipids and proteins combined together with hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions. We discussed micelles before, and these are designed a lot like those, hydrophobic tails on the inside, hydrophilic heads on the outside.

The larger lipoproteins with more lipids and less proteins will be less dense, whereas the smaller more protein rich lipoproteins will be more dense. The proteins are what determine the function of the lipoprotein because they act as markers or receptors.

Now that we know the basics, we can dive into the primary types of lipoproteins.

Click on the five hotspots in the photo below to learn more.

• Chylomicrons

    Chylomicrons are the lowest density lipoproteins, and they primarily transport dietary fats. They are cleared from the blood rapidly as part of food digestion. Their digestion results in the transport of fatty acids to the adipose tissue, heart, muscle, and liver.

  • Very Low Density Lipoproteins (VLDL)

    Triglycerides and cholesterol in excess of the liver’s own needs are exported into the blood in the form of very low-density lipoprotein.

    The triglycerides in VLDL are hydrolyzed by lipoprotein lipases on capillary surfaces, and the freed fatty acids are taken into the cells.

  • Intermediate Density Lipoproteins

    Once the fatty acids are removed from the triglycerides in the VLDLs, what is left is a cholesterol-rich remnant known as an intermediate-density lipoprotein.

    The IDLs can be taken up by the liver for processing or further processed into low-density lipoproteins.

  • Low-Density Lipoproteins (LDL)

    The major carrier of freshly synthesized cholesterol in the blood is low-density lipoprotein.

    The role of LDL is to transport cholesterol to the peripheral tissues and regulate de novo cholesterol synthesis at these sites.

    LDL is a sign of high concentrations of cholesterol being circulated for use in the body, High concentrations of LDL in the blood play a role in setting the conditions for a heart attack.

  • High Density Lipoproteins (HDL)

    High-density lipoprotein, or HDL, on the other hand, returns cholesterol to the liver in a process known as reverse cholesterol transport. It will pick up cholesterol released into the plasma from dying cells and from membranes undergoing turnover and return it to the liver for breakdown and excretion.

    HDL is considered the "good" cholesterol and is not associated with heart disease.
Do You Know?

Matching pairs
  • VLDL matches TAGs and cholesterol excess from liver into blood. triglycerides and cholesterol in excess of the liver's needs enter the blood in VLDLs
  • LDL matches Primary cholesterol transport. Cholesterol is transported from the liver to peripheral tissues via the LDL
  • HDL matches Reverse cholesterol transport. HDL is responsible for returning cholesterol to the liver for removal via bile and feces
  • chylomicron matches transport dietary fats. Dietary fats are transported via chylomicrons, which are digested rapidly

Cholesterol and Heart Disease

High cholesterol levels promote atherosclerosis, the leading cause of death in industrialized societies. Familial hypercholesterolemia is a genetic disorder that leads to susceptibility to atherosclerosis and is characterized by high concentraions of LDL in the blood (3-4 times the desired amount).

HDL can protect against atherosclerosis through removal of cholesterol from cells. Once in the liver, the cholesterol can be excrected from the body via the bile or feces. The higher a person's level of HDL, the more readily that person undergoes reverse cholersterol transport.
